# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.

- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".

- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why2: 'Missed only a little', 'caught only the gist' and 'missed most of it' are exactly how my hard-of-hearing users talk about a dinner table or a bar.
screens.why3: Anyone who sat in a group conversation this week knows how much of it they followed, like Kwame's '20% at best' while nodding along.
screens.why4: The five run from full to none on one scale, but 'Caught only the gist' and 'Missed most of it' can both be true of the same evening, since many of my users miss most words yet still get the topic.
screens.why5: It keeps my measure, how much of the conversation they followed, and leaks nothing about glasses or captions; only 'join' from my job is left implicit.
screens.why7: All five rungs grade how much was followed, best to worst; the first rung is today's way working and the last is failing outright; the line under 'Missed only a little' leaves two rungs that can refute the belief and three that can support it; and the bar names a rung on the final list.
screens.instead: Followed everything that was said · Missed only a little · ┄ line ┄ · Got the topic but lost the details · Missed most of it · Could not follow it at all

screens.why1: Choosing the interviewer before the link goes out belongs here, but for people who are deaf or hard of hearing the spoken voice is the least important part of the interview, so a voice picker feels slightly beside the point for my study.
screens.why2: Two named voices with a 5-second preview, and a hint that says plainly the questions are also written on screen and can be answered by typing or tapping, is clear on first read.
screens.why3: I can make this choice from my own taste and my knowledge of my users, since it asks nothing I would have to guess.
screens.why4: Daphne and Saskia are distinct, but for my respondents the real answer is often 'no voice, text and captions first', and that option is not on the screen; I only learn from the hint that the text is always there.
screens.why5: It keeps my actor, 'deaf or hard-of-hearing adults', and leaks nothing about the glasses or AirCaps to the people who will be asked.
screens.instead: How should Keel ask deaf or hard-of-hearing adults your questions? (Written on screen with captions, voice optional / Daphne's voice with captions / Saskia's voice with captions)

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks, it makes sense to decide how my respondents take the study before I send it.
screens.why2: The three choices are short and clear, and each one says plainly that the questions are written on screen and can be answered by typing, which is what matters for a deaf respondent.
screens.why3: I know my people: many are deaf or late-deafened, and some don't use their voice, so I can judge at once that reading and tapping suits them better than a spoken video interviewer.
screens.why4: Read-and-tap, an interviewer with on-screen text, and letting them choose are distinct and complete, and each keeps a typing path open for people who don't speak.
screens.why5: Nothing about the glasses or captions leaks into this; it only asks how my respondents answer, and my pick of Read and tap stands as typed.
screens.instead: How should deaf and hard-of-hearing adults answer? Read and tap (type in any box) / Daphne on video, with every question captioned on screen / Let them choose

screens.why1: After choosing who asks and how they answer, deciding who receives the link is the natural last step before sending interviews.
screens.why2: The first and third options are plain, but the second leans on Keel's own 'Contacts page' and 'a search' I have not seen in this flow, so I would read it twice; it also flips from 'I' to 'you' mid-option.
screens.why3: I know whether I am reaching deaf and hard-of-hearing people I know personally, a list, or a community group like an HLAA chapter or a Facebook group, so this is mine to answer.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover how I would reach people, but the voice is inconsistent ('I send' versus 'you send') and the Google sign-in detail on the open link is a caveat folded into an option rather than an option itself.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or study wording is touched; it is a pure sending choice and my pick, people I know by name, is kept.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? -- People I know by name (I send each their own link) / People from a Keel contact list (Keel makes a link per person, I send them) / A group I belong to (I post one open link; each person signs in with Google)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'People disagree' is stated with 'median 4 days out of 7' beside it, but a median of 4 sits inside my 4-to-7 belief, so that number reads as support; the figure that actually decides it, 4 of 7 at or beyond against a bar of 5, is only in the card below.
screens.why_b2: The tally '3 holding · 1 split · 7 people answered' is plain, but the Frequency card stacks median, below, at-or-beyond, bar and '1 short' in one line, and Importance repeats '7 of 7 put it in their two' twice, so I had to read it a second time.
screens.why_b3: Prevalence, Frequency, Importance and Current solution match what I checked, with my 4-to-7 days, my group-conversation problem and my segment; only the 'five things that are hard' framing on Importance is Keel's template.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what the split on Frequency means for AirCaps, for example whether to narrow to the people who struggle 4+ days a week or to sell on the hardest occasions rather than daily wear.
screens.why_b5: 7 people is visible, but it is never called a small sample, and 'Holding up' on 'at least 8 in 10 deaf and hard-of-hearing adults' rests on 7 answers with no caution.
screens.instead: Frequency split: 4 of 7 lose track on 4+ days, you needed 5, one short. With only 7 people, ask more before cutting it, or narrow AirCaps to the people whose week is full of group conversations.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "7 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows 7 cells for me on a 0 to 7 axis with my bar marked at 6 (at least 8 in 10), so what is counted, over how many, and where the bar sits are plain at once.
screens.why_b3: My band and my problem are there, but the belief line drops my segment's qualifier ("in the US who talk with hearing people every week"), so it reads as all deaf and hard-of-hearing adults, not the wedge I typed.
screens.why_b4: It tells me the problem is common among these 7 and sends me to Frequency and Importance to learn whether it is frequent and costly enough, which is the right next step given that the stage page shows Frequency in dispute.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible and the count line says outright that 7 is a small group, "a lean, not a call", so 7 of 7 is not oversold.
screens.instead: At least 8 in 10 deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week lost track of what people were saying in the last 7 days.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'People disagree' sits right beside the deciding count: 4 of 7 at or beyond my 4 days, against a bar of 5 of 7, one short.
screens.why_b2: The axis counts days out of 7 and the strip's marker counts people (5 of 7), so the two '5's need a second look; the axis also starts at a 0 nobody could pick, and the legend's 'at what you said' reads narrower than 'at or beyond'.
screens.why_b3: It is my Frequency belief with my 4 to 7 days out of 7, and 'lose track of what people were saying' is how my wearers talk about losing the conversation at a table.
screens.why_b4: 'Whether it matters is the next card' punts; it never says what a three-in-seven group at 1 to 3 days means for daily wear or for asking $20 a month for Pro.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 is kept and called 'a lean, not a call', but the Asked line's tag '— the most recent time it happened' misdescribes a 7-day count question as a most-recent-time one.
screens.instead: People disagree: 4 of 7 lost track of a conversation on 4 or more of the last 7 days, 1 short of your 5 of 7; the other 3 hit it 1 to 3 days a week, so ask whether those 3 would still wear the glasses daily before you lean on daily use and a monthly Pro plan.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside '7 of 7 put it in their two · bar 5 of 7', so I know it held and by what margin.
screens.why_b2: The bar on the strip and the 7 people are plain, but the caption says 'each picked two' while the bars add to 13, not 14, so I had to stop and work out that someone picked one and then Nothing else.
screens.why_b3: The title is Importance and the belief line is my problem in my words, keeping track of what hearing people say when the talk is too fast or too noisy, set against the five difficulties I listed.
screens.why_b4: The So line correctly says top two rather than first, but it doesn't tell me what to do: that following the talk is the problem to lead with, and that 'Getting a word in at the right moment' (3 picks) is a joining problem captions alone don't solve.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and the screen says outright 'a small group: a lean, not a call', so the unanimous result isn't sold as more than seven people.
screens.instead: Holding up: all 7 put following what hearing people say in their two (bar 5 of 7; one picked it alone, so 13 picks). A lean from 7. Lead with following the talk, and note 3 also want help getting a word in, which captions alone don't give.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding count, 6 of 7 said today's way falls short against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know the belief held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts one answer per person across my five rungs, the line under 'Missed only a little' marks where 'for' begins, and the strip shows 7 cells with the marker at 5, so what is counted, over how many and where the bar sits all read on first look.
screens.why_b3: 'Current solution' is my dimension, but the belief line's act, 'following a conversation with hearing people', drops the 'face-to-face' and 'join' of my job and the group, noisy occasion I meant, so it is recognisably mine but reworded.
screens.why_b4: 'Your solution is judged against this gap on the next study' points forward, but it doesn't say what the gap means for the glasses, for example that the gap sits in gist-level following, which is where captions should earn their place.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible throughout, the count line says plainly that seven is 'a lean, not a call', and the So line keeps its claim to 'these 7'.
screens.instead: Holding up, a lean on 7: 6 of 7 fell short of 'Missed only a little', split evenly between catching only the gist and missing most of it. The next study should test whether captions lift those six to 'Missed only a little' or better.

screens.why_b1: The verdict (Holding up) sits right beside the deciding number, 6 of 7 said today's way falls short against a bar of 5 of 7, and the line "Current solution held, 6 of 7" ties them together.
screens.why_b3: The dimension is Current solution and the belief line is the one I checked: for most deaf and hard-of-hearing adults, following a conversation with hearing people still falls short.
screens.why_b4: The screen never says what Tomás's answer means for AirCaps, for example whether to narrow the wedge away from people with one-sided loss who manage by choosing their seat, so I am left to work it out myself.
screens.why_b5: The n stays visible and nothing is overclaimed, but the header "When a line fails" sits over a line that held, and 7 people is never called a small sample.
screens.why_b6: Tomás's answer adds something I did not type: people deaf in one ear can get by with a seating tactic (end seat, good side) that works most of the time, which marks the edge of my segment.

screens.why1: As the first screen it checks I'm someone who talks with hearing people regularly, which is obviously the right gate for a study about following those conversations.
screens.why2: Talking with hearing people is exactly how I'd put it myself, and I can answer it on first reading.
screens.why3: I know straight away whether I talk with hearing people every week; I do, at work and in shops.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it cleanly for a gate, and the gate takes no escape.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's 'talk with hearing people every week' and nothing about a product reaches me.
screens.why6: Short, one question, two options anyone can hold when heard once.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I talk with hearing people every week, it makes sense to ask whether I lost the thread lately; that's the problem the study is about.
screens.why2: 'Lose track of what people were saying' is exactly how I'd say it to my audiologist or a friend, and I get it on first read or first hearing.
screens.why3: I know this week whether I lost the thread at the deli counter or my sister's dinner, so I can answer from my own week without guessing.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it and don't overlap; the chips beside it belong to the story box after a Yes, so they're not a fault of the gate.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but 'what people were saying' has lost the founder's face-to-face conversation with hearing people, so a captioned TV show or a muffled podcast could count as a Yes.
screens.why6: It's one short question with 'Yes or no' at the end, easy to hear once and answer.
screens.why7: It asks the act that hurts (losing track), not the routine, and a No is possible for someone whose talks this week were quiet one-to-ones, but the face-to-face, with-hearing-people condition is dropped, so Yes can come from outside the founder's problem.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you lose track of a conversation with hearing people? Yes / No

screens.why1: Right after I said yes to losing track this week, asking how many days it happened is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: Losing track of what people were saying is exactly how I'd put it myself, and the question is short and clear the first time I read it.
screens.why3: I know which days I was at work, at the shop or out with hearing friends, so I can count the days it happened instead of guessing a number of times.
screens.why4: One button for each day from 1 to 7, none overlapping, with I can't recall kept apart, covers every true answer for someone who already said yes.
screens.why5: It only asks about my own conversations, and nothing about a product, captions or the founder's terms comes through.
screens.why6: Heard aloud it's one short question, then 'say a number from 1 to 7' and the one escape, which is easy to hold and answer.
screens.why7: The options are on the one measure the card names (days of the window, 1 to 7, unit said once, no zero) and the required I can't recall escape is there, so a founder low of 2 or more can be supported or refuted.

screens.why1: Right after counting the days I lost track, it makes sense to ask which part of that I'd most like made easier, thinking of my last conversation.
screens.why2: Lip-reading, missing jokes, getting a word in and losing the start of a point are all things I'd say myself, so I can answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: Every row is something I meet myself, face to face with hearing people, so I'm answering from my own last conversation rather than guessing.
screens.why4: 'Keeping track of what hearing people say' covers missing jokes and losing the start of a point, so it overlaps them, and 'Missing jokes' reads backwards after 'made easier' (I don't want missing jokes made easier).
screens.why5: Nothing about any product or company reaches me, and the founder's 'losing track of what people say' is still here as 'keeping track'.
screens.why6: One short question and five short phrases I can hold, with 'none of these' said last, though 'recovering after missing the start of a point' is the longest to hear.
screens.why7: The own row is there and not first, and the escape is right, so the belief can go either way; but the own row is near the whole job and swallows two rivals, and one rival is a bad outcome rather than a task, which bends the shape rules.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Keeping up when several people talk at once · Catching the joke before the group moves on · Getting a word in at the right moment · Reading lips when faces turn away · Catching up after missing the start of a point · None of these

screens.why1: Right after I picked what I'd most like made easier, asking how my last conversation with hearing people actually went is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: The anchor says 'your last conversation' and then the question says 'a conversation with hearing people', so I had to reread to check whether it meant that same conversation or some other one, since my last one may have been with deaf friends.
screens.why3: I know exactly how much I caught the last time I talked with hearing people; that's my week, every week.
screens.why4: Five clear steps from following everything to not following at all, none overlapping, in words I'd use myself, and 'I can't recall' fits because nobody else can follow a conversation for me.
screens.why5: It's about following a conversation with hearing people, which is my life, and nothing about a product or plan reaches me.
screens.why6: Heard aloud, 'conversation' twice in two breaths with a mismatched frame is clumsy, though the five options themselves are short and easy to hold.
screens.why7: Every rung is how much of the conversation I followed, one measure, five in order from the working first rung to failing outright, a working rung above any line and shortfalls below, and the card's escape for an act you can't hand off.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. How much of it did you follow? Followed everything that was said; missed only a little; caught only the gist; missed most of it; could not follow it at all; or I can't recall.
